# Probes on the 7600X, 2026-10-08

The records of the probes that found `inner` moves a two-thread bench's time per step, taken
before the sweep in [random-inner.md](../../notes/random-inner.md) and cited by it and by
`TODO.md`. Each file is one invocation, its name the setting it ran at.

- Source: commit `a946d7c1`, jj change `rrwqouqq`, the plain `iiac-perf` 0.28.23, binary
  `7715ab993ac3b78c`, built on the 3900X.
- Host: the 7600X, the clock pinned at 4701 MHz. `ccx` is CPUs 5 and 4, `smt` CPUs 5 and 11.
- Every run `--run-sleep 100-200ms`, ten runs an invocation unless said. `$B` is
  `zcr-mpsc-v4-2t-single-sos-futex-spntfe`.
- The files were written on the 7600X under `~/iiac-perf-data/` and each record carries that
  path. They were copied here unchanged.

## The environment's size and address randomization, `lay-*`

`lay-NNNN-a.jsonl`, 110 runs, 14:44Z to 14:49Z: `$B` on `ccx`, the environment padded by a
variable `PAD` of `NNNN` bytes, 0 to 4096 in eleven steps, address randomization on, the
default. The `inner` is the harness's own.

`lay-NNNN-r.jsonl` and `lay-NNNN-s.jsonl`, 40 runs: the same at 0 and 64 bytes with address
randomization off, `setarch -R`, `r` and `s` being two invocations of it.

```
for n in 0000 0008 0016 0032 0064 0128 0256 0512 1024 2048 4096; do
  PAD=$(head -c $((10#$n)) /dev/zero | tr "\0" x) iiac-perf $B --pin-cpus ccx \
    --run-sleep 100-200ms --record-file lay-$n-a.jsonl
done
for n in 0000 0064; do for r in r s; do
  PAD=$(head -c $((10#$n)) /dev/zero | tr "\0" x) setarch -R iiac-perf $B --pin-cpus ccx \
    --run-sleep 100-200ms --record-file lay-$n-$r.jsonl
done; done
```

## `inner` fixed at 5 to 8, `inn-*`

`inn-I-P.jsonl`, 120 runs, 14:50Z to 14:54Z: `$B` on `ccx` at `--inner I`, three passes `P`
of `a`, `b`, `c`, each pass in the order 6, 7, 5, 8. Thirty runs a value.

```
for p in a b c; do for i in 6 7 5 8; do
  iiac-perf $B --pin-cpus ccx --run-sleep 100-200ms --inner $i --record-file inn-$i-$p.jsonl
done; done
```

## `inner` fixed at 1 to 16, `swp-*`

`swp-W-PL-II.jsonl`, 240 runs, 15:01Z to 15:09Z, the table in `TODO.md`'s entry "The period of 4
in a can-sleep ring's level": five runs at each `--inner` from 1 to 16, ascending, of three
cases, `so` on `ccx`, `sos-futex` on `ccx`, and `sos-futex` on `smt`.

```
for i in 01 02 03 04 05 06 07 08 09 10 11 12 13 14 15 16; do
  for c in so:ccx sos-futex:ccx sos-futex:smt; do w=${c%%:*}; pl=${c##*:}
    iiac-perf zcr-mpsc-v4-2t-single-$w-spntfe --pin-cpus $pl --runs 5 \
      --run-sleep 100-200ms --inner $((10#$i)) --record-file swp-$w-$pl-$i.jsonl
  done
done
```

## `min-now` at fixed `inner`, `mn-*`

`mn-auto.jsonl`, three runs at the harness's own `inner`, 21. `mn-I-P.jsonl`, 180 runs, 15:09Z
to 15:16Z: `min-now` on `smt` at `--inner` 10, 14, 18, 20, 21, 22, 24, 30, and 42, two passes,
the source of the cycle's `18.27 + 18.47 / inner` ns.

```
for p in a b; do for i in 10 14 18 20 21 22 24 30 42; do
  iiac-perf min-now --pin-cpus smt --run-sleep 100-200ms --inner $i --record-file mn-$i-$p.jsonl
done; done
```

## The stopped large sweep, `partial-big-sweep-7600x.jsonl`

800 runs, 16:08Z to 16:35Z: pass `a` of a sweep of five two-thread benches on `smt` and `ccx`,
five runs at each of 24 `inner` values from 1 to 24 in a scrambled order, stopped after 16 of
them for its length. `Single` and `Multi` over one segment, each over `SpinOnly` and
`SpinOrSleep<Futex>` spinning forever, and `Single` over `Sleep<Futex>`:

```
T2="zcr-mpsc-v4-2t-single-so-spntfe zcr-mpsc-v4-2t-single-sos-futex-spntfe \
    zcr-mpsc-v4-2t-multi-1seg-so-spntfe zcr-mpsc-v4-2t-multi-1seg-sos-futex-spntfe \
    zcr-mpsc-v4-2t-single-slp-futex-slptfe"
for i in 13 4 22 9 1 18 7 24 11 2 16 5 20 14 3 23 8 12 19 6 21 10 17 15; do
  iiac-perf $T2 --pin-cpus smt,ccx --runs 5 --run-sleep 100-200ms --inner $i --tag pass=a \
    --record-file inner-sweep-7600x.jsonl
done
```

It was renamed `partial-big-sweep-7600x.jsonl` when stopped. On the `ccx` pair a dozen or so of
its runs read well above the other collections at the same `inner`, which none of them show.

content.content:
A two-thread bench on a ring that can sleep reads low when `inner`, the steps timed back to back
in one sample, is a multiple of 4, and high when it is odd (wink, 2026-10-08, after the overnight
sessions on the landed names disagreed with the first session). The harness sizes `inner` by
itself in every run, so the level a bench reports depends on where that sizing lands.

The sweep, 7600X, `zcr-mpsc-v4-2t-single-*-spntfe`, `--inner` fixed, five runs each, level in ns.
The records are in `tmp/layout-7600x/` on the 3900X, not committed:

| `inner` | `so`, ccx | `sos-futex`, ccx | `sos-futex`, smt |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 90.6 | 93.0 | 62.6 |
| 2 | 75.2 | 78.0 | 53.6 |
| 16 | 69.2 | 68.1 | 45.9 |

What is established:

- the level follows `inner` and nothing else tried. Thirty runs each at 5, 6, 7 and 8 on the ccx
  pair read 73.1, 70.6, 75.5 and 67.1 ns, 27 or more of each 30 within 0.6 ns
- the environment's size does not move it, padded from 0 to 4096 bytes, and neither does turning
The disagreement was two overnight sessions on one binary, five invocations of ten runs and one
of fifty, against each other and against the session in
[mpsc-v4-mode-waits.md](mpsc-v4-mode-waits.md), on two-thread benches at cross-core placements.
Three probes on the 7600X `ccx` pair, on `sos-futex-spntfe`, found what moved the time per step.
Their records are not committed:

- The environment's size does not. Padded by 0 to 4096 bytes in eleven steps, ten runs each, 107

## What it does not hold

- `Multi`, the `smt` pair for two threads, and `inner` past 16. A larger sweep was stopped for
  its length, and its one pass, 800 runs, is not committed.
- The 3900X and the Pi 5.
- Why repeating one burst length gives the ring that can sleep a period of 4, and what sets
  which of the two rates a run lands on.
    later installed first.
- `tmp/runs-debug.patch` is wink's two debug prints in `src/runs.rs`, set aside at the closing so
  its commit did not carry them.
- The stopped sweep's one pass, 800 runs, five two-thread benches on `smt` and `ccx` at 16 of 24
  `inner` values, is `tmp/layout-7600x/partial-big-sweep-7600x.jsonl` on the 3900X, with the
  probes' records beside it, none committed.
- The 7600X has `iiac-perf-dev` 0.28.24-2 in `~/.cargo/bin`, copied there for the random runs,
  beside the plain `iiac-perf` 0.28.23. The Pi 5 and the 3900X have no dev build of this cycle
  beyond the 3900X's own.
- The overnight sessions of 2026-10-08 on the landed names, five invocations of ten runs and one
  of fifty per host, `--run-sleep 100-200ms`, are in `tmp/session-<host>-20261008/` on the 3900X
  and not committed. `tmp/cmp3.py` compares them with the first session. The v4 note's tables are
  not rebuilt from them, held by [The period of 4](#the-period-of-4-in-a-can-sleep-rings-level).

### figures draws time per step against inner

A table of medians hides the period of 4 under the overhead's fall with `inner`, and its source
can be misread, as the period-of-4 entry's table and its thirty-run bullet were (wink,
2026-10-15, asking for a graph of all the data). A throwaway drawing of every run on the 7600X
`ccx` pair, `tmp/inner-raw.png` and `tmp/inner-overhead-off.png` on the 3900X, showed it at
once: the fixed collections agree, `sos-futex-spntfe` zigzags by `inner` modulo 4, random lengths
are smooth, and over 1-32 the runs split into two rates.

- `iiac-perf figures` learns the kind of figure, `--figure`, the block means its first, and
  panels that hold dots and a categorical colour and a legend as well as lines
- time per step against `inner`, every run a dot coloured by `inner` modulo 4, fixed runs as
  points and random runs as a line a run through their lengths
- the same with the harness overhead off, from `linear-regression`'s own arithmetic, so the
  figure and the command cannot disagree
- a random run's slope, one dot a run, to show the two rates
- the figures go into [random-inner.md](notes/random-inner.md) as committed SVGs drawn from
  `records/`, with the commands that redraw them

lastPrompt: I don't think the title needs to change. Maybe the data goes in the next cycle??? On the graph the the substracted overhead seems wrong, with the raising "tail" that seems weird. Also the slow startup…

content.text:
Taking your three points in turn.

**1. Data now or in the next cycle.** I agree it fits the next cycle better. That cycle is "a graph of all the data", and the figures will read these records, so committing them there gives the data a reason to exist in the same commit that uses it. It also keeps this step to what its title says.

Moving it means setting aside the parts I just added: the `records/probes-7600x-20261008/` directory with its README, the "now committed" wording in the note and `TODO.md`, the removed continuation-note bullet, and the data bullet in Ladder details. They'd be saved as a patch in `tmp/` and reapplied in the next cycle. The source labels in the period-of-4 entry would stay, pointing at the `tmp/` files as before. Your call, but I lean towards moving it.

**2. The rising tail with the overhead taken off.** I don't think the subtraction is wrong. The rise is already in the raw data, and the subtraction only makes it plainer.
- In the raw graph, every random 1-16 run also rises, from about 74.5 ns at length 5 to 75.2 at 16. Raw time per step should fall as the length grows, because the fixed overhead is shared over more steps. If it rises anyway, the cost of a step itself is going up with burst length in those runs.
- Taking the overhead off removes the falling part, so the rise underneath shows more: about 73 to 76 ns.
- Could the overhead be badly wrong instead? An error δ in the overhead bends the curve by δ/`inner`. To make a 3 ns rise between lengths 4 and 16, δ would have to be about 16 ns, meaning the true overhead is near 2 ns rather than 18. `min-now` measures 18.2 to 18.5 ns where a line holds to 0.01%, so that isn't plausible.
- What is odd: the two 1-32 runs on the upper rate don't rise over the same lengths. We think a sample's cost may depend on the samples just before it, so the span itself shapes the curve. That's something to look at in the next cycle, not now.

**3. "Slow startup" and warmup.** The x axis in these graphs is burst length, not time. With random `inner`, samples of length 1, 2, 3 are interleaved through the whole run, after warmup, so their high cost isn't the run starting up. It's what a short burst costs every time it happens: the about 10 ns once a sample that we think is the ring starting a burst. Warmup would show up over time, which is what `iiac-perf figures`' existing block-means figure draws. If you want to check warmup, that's the figure to look at, and nothing in these graphs points to warmup being too short.

In short: moving the data to the next cycle is cleaner. The rising tail is real, already there before the subtraction. The high cost at short lengths is a per-burst cost, not warmup.

content.text:
The data is moved out:
- `records/probes-7600x-20261008/` is removed from the working copy. The original files are all still in `tmp/layout-7600x/`.
- The README I wrote is saved as `tmp/next-cycle-data/probes-README.md`.
- The text that pointed at the directory is reverted. The note and `TODO.md` say "not committed" again, and the period-of-4 labels now point at `tmp/layout-7600x/swp-*` and `inn-*`.
- The continuation note is restored, with one addition: these records go into `records/probes-7600x-20261008/` in the figures cycle, with that saved README.
- The Ladder details keep only the source-labelling bullet.

Fast validation passed.

**Is fixed versus random the only variable?** No. I checked the timed loop (`src/harness.rs:701-713`). Both kinds call the same `record_sample(bench, length, …)`, so the timed code is the same. But several other things change along with "random":

1. **The binary.** Fixed used plain 0.28.23, random used dev 0.28.24-2. This one is controlled: the random set included fixed runs at 7 and 8 with the new binary, and they read as the old binary did (76.0 and 67.0 against 75.7 and 66.9).
2. **Repetition.** With a fixed length, every sample follows one of the same length. This is the variable the note credits.
3. **The loop's exit can no longer be predicted.** With a fixed count, the CPU learns where the inner loop ends. With a random one it guesses wrong about once a sample. That goes along with repetition, and the current data can't separate the two. A missed guess costs about the same every sample, so it should mostly land in the per-sample part, but we think it could also take part in the period of 4, if that comes from how the loop runs.
4. **One process across all lengths.** Each random run measures every length within one process, so each line shares that process's state, its address layout and which of the two rates it landed on. Its points are smooth partly by construction. Each fixed point is a separate process.

Point 4 doesn't explain the fixed zigzag away. Thirty separate processes at one value agree to within 0.6 ns, and four collections agree with each other, so the zigzag is reproducible and not process noise. But it does mean "random is smoother" is part repetition, part predictability, and part one process per line. The note's line "the period of 4 followed the repetition" claims more than the data separates.

Two cheap tests would separate them, for the next cycle:
- **`--inner 7-8`**, random between just 7 and 8. If its two per-length values stay near the fixed 75.7 and 66.9, the cost follows the length. If they come together, it's the repetition or the predictability.
- **A fixed cycle of lengths** instead of random ones: varied but predictable. That needs a small harness change.

When this step's description is written, I'd soften the note's claim to "the period goes when lengths are random, and whether from the repetition or the loop's predictability is not separated". That's one sentence in this step, and you can say no.

In short: random also brings an unpredictable loop exit and one process per line, so the smoothness isn't proof that repetition alone caused the period. Two small tests in the next cycle can tell them apart.

content.content:
- A sweep, each run at one fixed `inner` and the runs stepping it across a range, shows the
  dependence has a period of 4.
- Runs in which each sample picks its `inner` at random from a span remove the period, so the
  result no longer hangs on one value.
- They do not make every run agree: over 1-32 a run lands on one of two rates about 6 ns a step
  apart.
- `linear-regression`, `lr` for short and first named `fit`, reads both, and with the harness
  overhead of about 18 ns taken off gives a step's cost where a line holds.

Whether random `inner` makes separate invocations agree is not tested here.
---
## Random per sample

A run at a fixed `inner` repeats one burst length, so the sweep cannot say whether a two-thread
bench's cost follows the length or the repetition. `--inner 1-16` picks each sample's length at
random from the span, and the record holds the samples and their summed time at each length.

---
- One thread: both ways give `min-now` 18.26 ns a step and about 18.4 ns a sample, the two
  slopes 0.008 ns apart. The regression holds and the two ways agree.
- The period of 4 followed the repetition. Fixed, `sos-futex-spntfe`'s residuals by `inner`
  modulo 4 are -31.7, +14.9, +0.3 and +16.4 ns a sample, a period that accounts for 71% of the
  other pass's residual scatter. Random over 1-16 they are -0.9, +1.4, -0.1 and -0.4 ns, and
  `linear-regression` finds no period in any random group.
- What is left is smooth. A sample of one step sits 10 ns over the line for `sos-futex-spntfe`
  and 15 ns for `so-spntfe`, the next few under it, and from about 8 steps the time per step is flat
  to 0.3 ns. So the short lengths bend the line, and over 1-32, where they are a smaller share,
  the halves come within 1.4%.
---

So for one thread the regression gives the step's cost and the sample's overhead. For two
threads random lengths remove the period, and what remains, a bend at short lengths and
two rates a run may land on, still keeps a line from holding in most groups.

## With the overhead taken off

---
([random-inner.md](notes/random-inner.md)):

- the period follows the repetition of one length and not the length. With `inner` random per
  sample from 1-16 the residuals by `inner` modulo 4 are within 1.4 ns a sample, where fixed
  they run from -31.7 to +16.4, and `fit` finds no period in any random group
- a second thing came out: over 1-32 a run lands on one of two rates about 6 ns a step apart,
  eight runs of ten on the lower, and over 1-16 all ten on the upper. Nothing says what sets it

  the halves come within 1.4%.

# Commit model

Two commit bodies from the `config loader` cycle in [cycle-model.md](cycle-model.md), shown as
specimens rather than a skeleton: a work rung's body and a bookend's. Copy the shape, not the
words. The rules are in [Commit-body form](prose.md#commit-body-form).

## A work rung

Title: `refactor: split loader from parser`

```
Config loading and parsing are one function, so the CLI cannot load a
config without parsing it and a test cannot parse one without a file on
disk. The move into its own module is what forces the split.

* The two jobs share one function and one error type.
  - `config::loader` finds and reads the file and returns the text with
    its path, so a caller that only wants to know which file was read
    stops there.
  - `config::parser` takes text and returns the schema, so a test hands
    it a string and never touches the filesystem.
* `main` still reaches into the parse result by field.
  - `main` calls `config::load` and receives the schema, so the field
    access moves behind the module boundary and the CLI no longer knows
    the file's shape.
```

The intro states this commit's problem and defines "split", the word the title assumes. Each `*`
is one facet of it, each `-` under a `*` answers that facet, and nothing names a file that the
diff already lists.

## A bookend

Title: `refactor: extract config loader opening`

```
Opens the cycle "refactor: extract config loader". Its record is the
In Progress block in TODO.md.
```

A bookend resolves no problem of its own, so its body is the intro paragraph alone, naming the
cycle by its title and pointing at its record. The closing's body is the same shape with "Closes".

### Commit-body form

The specimen is [commit-model.md](commit-model.md). A commit body is the [Problem-first
shape](#problem-first-shape) with one addition: a body whose
problem has several sub-problems arranges them by a fixed recursion, so a reader knows what any
bullet is from its marker and its depth. The earlier statement, "a problem statement then a solution
statement, both broad", left that arrangement to taste, and taste converged slowly and separately.

- **An intro paragraph states the general problem**, and defines any word the title assumes. It is
  mandatory. [Prose form](#prose-form) wants it regardless, and a body opening on a bullet is a body

  resolves is describing something larger than the commit.

  not a grab-bag of unrelated fixes. A body reaching for unrelated problem bullets is usually asking
  to be more than one commit.

  `*` above it reads as a solution to nothing, so there are no top-level solutions: a solution that
  retires every facet at once is written under each, or the facets are one.

  form, the general form at its smallest.

  its body is the intro paragraph alone, naming the cycle by its title and pointing at its record,

read as plain text, in `jj log` and in terminals, where the markers survive, and if a renderer ever
flattens them the indentation still carries the structure. So the mixed markers are deliberate, and
a linter's consistent-marker rule is wrong to normalize them.

content.content:
## Comparing implementations: least significant change

How to decide whether implementation A is really faster than B
at 95% confidence, worked from a six-run tp-pc series on
r5-7600x (2026-07-13).

The unit of replication is the **run**, not the sample. A run's
millions of samples make its within-run standard error
microscopic; what dominates comparison error is run-to-run
systematic drift (mode mix, frequency regime, calibration).
So compare per-run statistics:

- Do n runs of A and n of B — n is the **replication count per
  implementation** (n=5 → 10 runs total) — **interleaved**
  (A,B,A,B,...) so thermal / frequency drift hits both arms
  alike; same machine, same duration, same pinning; discard an
  initial warm-up run.
- Take one statistic per run (today `mean min-p99`; the
  trimmed p10-p90 row when it lands), giving n values per arm.
- Two-sample t at 95%: LSC = t(0.975, 2n-2) * s * sqrt(2/n),
this box's 100-block config, its 1-10 ms sleep included in every duration:

| run                                     | plain 0.28.10 |     before fix | after fix |
|-----------------------------------------|--------------:|---------------:|----------:|
| `mpsc-2t -d 3` pinned, six runs         |     3.8-3.9 s |   6.5-34.2 s * | 3.8-4.9 s |
| `mpsc-2t -d 10 --blocks 100`, three runs |             - |    8.1-72.3 s  | 10.6-12.1 s |

\* measured at the 10-block config, whose sleeps cost about 0.5 s less.

The cap cut one block in the three `-d 10` runs and none in `min-now`, so counts stay equal
wherever the median estimate holds, and the cap is the backstop for a bench that changes state
after its warmup.

cat >> notes/design.md <<'E'

## The cost of a step: a line through sample time against inner

A bench's time per step is a sample's time divided by `inner`, so it carries the harness's
overhead, the clock reads around the sample, shared out over the steps. `linear-regression`, `lr`
for short, separates the two by fitting `sample time = intercept + slope x inner` over runs at
several lengths, fixed per run or random per sample. The reasons, from `feat: fit, the cost of a
step from samples of many lengths` (2026-10-08 to 2026-10-15), with what it found in
[random-inner.md](random-inner.md):

- The slope, not a subtraction. A frame measured alone can cost differently from one in place,
  and a large `inner` that shrinks the share turns every bench into a burst bench, so the step's
  cost is read off a fitted line.
- Run means are the points. A run's blocks share its level and add rows, not points, so counting
  them would shrink the uncertainty without cause. Each length's value is `analyze`'s trimmed mean
  over its runs, by the same `trim_runs`, since a disturbance only adds time and least squares is
  pulled hard by a stray, and the untrimmed line is printed beside it.
- A line is tested, not assumed. The line is refitted over each half of the lengths, and where
  the halves' slopes differ by more than 1% and more than the runs' scatter allows, no cost is
  named: a systematic effect of `inner` makes the slope something other than a step's cost.
- A period is proven on the other pass. The residuals are grouped by `inner` modulo k, and k is
  scored by how much of the other pass's scatter one pass's group means account for, since more
  groups always fit their own noise. The smallest k near the best is named, a k must come round
  three times, and neighbouring residuals that agree with no k passing are reported as slow
  structure.
- The overhead is the host's, one number for every bench. The harness wraps every sample in the
  same clock reads, so the overhead is `min-now`'s intercept on the same host where its line
  holds, or `--overhead NS`, and it is taken off each length to give the step's cost there.
  Whether a clock read costs the same after a ring step as after another clock read is not
  measured.
- Fixed and random lengths are not mixed in one fit. A slope from random lengths is a step's cost
  among mixed bursts, not the time per step at any one `inner`, and the overhead read from each
  differs, 18.53 ns fixed and 18.16 ns random on the 7600X.
E

toolUseResult.oldString:
A `fit` subcommand that reads records taken at several fixed `inner` values and fits a line
through sample time against `inner`. The slope is the cost of one step and the intercept the cost
of one sample with no steps in it. It shows its working, each `inner` beside the line's value, so
the arithmetic can be followed. The records it is written against are collected first, a sweep of
`--inner` on the 7600X, and committed. The harness then learns to pick `inner` at random per
sample from a range, so one run holds samples of many lengths, and `fit` reads those records as
well.
toolUseResult.newString:
What was done:

- A sweep of fixed `inner` on the 7600X was taken and committed, now
  `records/inner-fixed-7600x.jsonl`.
- The harness learned `--inner` as a span, each sample picking its length at random, the record
  carrying a count and a summed time for each length. Runs over 1-16, 1-32, and 20-120 are
  `records/inner-random-7600x.jsonl`.
- A subcommand first named `fit`, then `linear-regression`, `lr` for short, fits sample time
  against `inner` over run means, trimmed across runs, and shows each length beside the line. It
  tests the line by refitting its halves, names a period scored on the other pass, and names no
  cost where a line does not hold.
- The harness overhead is taken as known, `min-now`'s intercept on the same host or
  `--overhead`, and taken off each length to give a step's cost there.
- What it found is [random-inner.md](notes/random-inner.md): one thread holds a line, 18.26 ns a
  step and 18.5 ns a sample; a fixed `inner` gives the ring that can sleep a period of 4, which
  disappears with random lengths; two-thread runs land on one of two rates and mostly hold no
  line. Its design reasons are in [The cost of a
  step](notes/design.md#the-cost-of-a-step-a-line-through-sample-time-against-inner).

content.content:
## Cycle bookmarks: create and land

The mechanics behind [Cycles run on a bookmark](../AGENTS.md#cycles-run-on-a-bookmark). That section
holds the rule and when it applies, and this one holds the commands
([why](rationale.md#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land)).

**Create**, at the cycle's opening, with the bookmark named by the cycle title's slug (the anchor
algorithm in [Markdown anchor links](notes.md#markdown-anchor-links), so the block's title heading
and the bookmark derive from one bare title):

- `jj git push --named <bookmark>=@- -R .` is the common case: it creates the bookmark at the last
  committed change and publishes it in one invocation.
- Any other revision works as the `=<rev>` right-hand side. When `<rev>` is not `@-`, follow with
  `jj new <rev> -R .` so the working copy actually sits on the new line. Otherwise the bookmark
  exists and the next commit lands somewhere else.
- `jj bookmark set <bookmark> -r <rev> -R .` creates it without publishing, for a line that is not
  ready to be seen.

**Land**, once the close-out is approved: the sequence that makes the cycle permanent. Every
`jj git push` in it is a push under [Approval per push](../AGENTS.md#before-any-push) and [Hard
stop after the final push](../AGENTS.md#at-rest-push-stop-squash-push), its own approval, the
closing words before the final invocation, silence after ([At
rest](../AGENTS.md#at-rest-push-stop-squash-push)):

1. Restore the plain name, when the project renamed ([Dev artifact
   name](versioning.md#dev-artifact-name)): rename `<name>-dev` back to `<name>` in the manifest,
   `vc-x1 validate --fast` so the lockfile follows, and `jj squash` folds the edit into the closing
   (`@` sits directly above it).
2. Reshape per the recorded choice: trapezoid runs the [recipe below](#trapezoid-close-out-recipe),
   keep separate needs nothing. A single-step cycle has no choice recorded and its one commit lands
   as it is.
3. Fast-forward: `jj bookmark set main -r <closeout> -R .`, then `jj git push --bookmark main -R .`.
   This push publishes the reshaped commit, so the topic bookmark itself is never re-pushed.
4. Install: promote the artifact from `main`, the cycle's last act, run when nothing can enter the
   cycle anymore.
5. Delete the bookmark, locally and remotely: `jj bookmark delete <bookmark>`, then
   `jj git push --bookmark <bookmark>` ([Bookmark per
   cycle](../AGENTS.md#cycles-run-on-a-bookmark)). The long-lived case below gets the same
   disposal once fully merged.

- The fast-forward needs no `--allow-backwards`. Needing it means the bookmark is not a descendant
  of `main`, and the situation wants a look, not a flag.
- Landing is the moment the cycle's commits become permanent. No record cites their SHAs
  ([Cycle-record](../AGENTS.md#cycle-record)): the landed commits are the record.

**Reshape**, while the bookmark is a draft ([Cycles run on a
bookmark](../AGENTS.md#cycles-run-on-a-bookmark)):

content.content:
## Trapezoid close-out recipe

The reshape behind the trapezoid shape, run at [Land](#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land) step 2: the
close-out commit, pushed linearly by the closing rung, becomes a merge whose first parent is the
trunk line and whose second parent is the cycle's ladder. Nothing here publishes, the merge goes out
with Land's fast-forward.

```
  main line   ...--<base>------------------<closeout>--
                      \                    /
  ladder             <rung-1>--...--<tip>-+
```

- `<base>`: the **parent of the ladder's first rung**, the trunk position when the cycle opened. It
  becomes the first parent. Not always the previous close-out: a cycle landed linearly since
  (keep-separate shape, or a single-step cycle) sits on the trunk line and must stay there.
- `<tip>`: the cycle's last commit before the close-out. It becomes the second parent.
- `<closeout>`: the close-out commit, reshaped here.

1. `jj rebase -r <closeout> --onto <base> --onto <tip>`: `<closeout>` becomes the merge. Parent
   order is the argument order.
2. `jj new <closeout>`: an empty `@` above the merge. The bookmark followed the rewrite on its own.
   What step 1 leaves misplaced is the working copy: `jj rebase -r` re-parents descendants onto the
   rebased commit's old parent, so the empty `@` lands beside the merge on `<tip>` and the tree
   reverts to pre-close-out content, which looks alarming and is not.
3. Verify two parents: `jj log -r <closeout> -T 'parents.map(|p| p.change_id().short(8))'` must list
   both. jj preserves the second parent even though `<base>` is an ancestor of `<tip>` (observed at
   three consecutive close-outs), but a collapsed merge is indistinguishable from a correct one in
   `jj log --no-graph`.

Details:

- **Trailers survive.** The restore's squash and the reshape change `<closeout>`'s SHA but not its
  change id, so the `ochid:` trailers stamped at the closing push stay valid in both directions.
- **Immutability.** No flag is needed: a topic bookmark's commits are not on `trunk()` until Land's
  fast-forward.

Recovery:

- **Nothing is published until Land's fast-forward**, so the whole reshape is undoable with
  `jj undo` / `jj op restore`.
- **A collapsed or mis-parented merge**: undo and redo step 1 with the corrected revisions. Do not
  land a shape you did not intend. After the fast-forward the remote boundary is crossed and
  recovery is forward-only.
- **Working copy left beside the merge** (step 2 skipped): `jj new <closeout>` after the fact. Any
  commit made in the meantime branches off `<tip>` and needs a rebase onto the merge.

- **Promotion**: plain `<name>` updates only by an explicit act: a separate clone built at the
  chosen commit with the plain name (or a copy of the dev binary), never by the per-commit flow's
  install.

**Single-name variant**: a repo striving to release makes the package name the binary's name, plain
`<name>` on `main` only:

- **The opening renames**: its bump sets `<name>-dev` beside the suffixed version, and every rung
  and the closing build under the dev name, the closing over the bare version.
- **Land restores**: the rename back to `<name>` is Land's act, so the stable name is only ever
  installed from what `main` will carry.
- **A build script guards the pairing** on every cargo verb: a suffixed version under the stable
  name fails the build, so no mid-cycle install can clobber the consumers' binary.

## Unique per commit (preference, not requirement)

Our general notion is that the version-of-record should change on **every commit**, so a built or
running artifact identifies the exact commit it came from.

lines: [[package]]
-name = "iiac-perf"
+name = "iiac-perf-dev"
dependencies = [
"clap",
"clap_complete",
[package]
-name = "iiac-perf"
+name = "iiac-perf-dev"
edition = "2024"

description = "Latency microbenchmark harness for Rust: percentile-band histograms of raw measurements, adaptive loop sizing, per-thread CPU pinning, and per-run grades for the workload and the machine. First benches measure inter-/intra-application communication (IIAC)."
The cap cut one block in the three `-d 10` runs and none in `min-now`, so counts stay equal
wherever the median estimate holds, and the cap is the backstop for a bench that changes state
after its warmup.
-## The cost of a step: a line through sample time against inner
-A bench's time per step is a sample's time divided by `inner`, so it carries the harness's
-overhead, the clock reads around the sample, shared out over the steps. `linear-regression`, `lr`
-for short, separates the two by fitting `sample time = intercept + slope x inner` over runs at
-several lengths, fixed per run or random per sample. The reasons, from `feat: fit, the cost of a
-step from samples of many lengths` (2026-10-08 to 2026-10-15), with what it found in
-[random-inner.md](random-inner.md):
-- The slope, not a subtraction. A frame measured alone can cost differently from one in place,
-  and a large `inner` that shrinks the share turns every bench into a burst bench, so the step's
-  cost is read off a fitted line.
-- Run means are the points. A run's blocks share its level and add rows, not points, so counting
-  them would shrink the uncertainty without cause. Each length's value is `analyze`'s trimmed mean
-  over its runs, by the same `trim_runs`, since a disturbance only adds time and least squares is
-  pulled hard by a stray, and the untrimmed line is printed beside it.
-- A line is tested, not assumed. The line is refitted over each half of the lengths, and where
-  the halves' slopes differ by more than 1% and more than the runs' scatter allows, no cost is
-  named: a systematic effect of `inner` makes the slope something other than a step's cost.
-- A period is proven on the other pass. The residuals are grouped by `inner` modulo k, and k is
-  scored by how much of the other pass's scatter one pass's group means account for, since more
-  groups always fit their own noise. The smallest k near the best is named, a k must come round
-  three times, and neighbouring residuals that agree with no k passing are reported as slow
-  structure.
-- The overhead is the host's, one number for every bench. The harness wraps every sample in the
-  same clock reads, so the overhead is `min-now`'s intercept on the same host where its line
-  holds, or `--overhead NS`, and it is taken off each length to give the step's cost there.
-  Whether a clock read costs the same after a ring step as after another clock read is not
-  measured.
-- Fixed and random lengths are not mixed in one fit. A slope from random lengths is a step's cost
-  among mixed bursts, not the time per step at any one `inner`, and the overhead read from each
-  differs, 18.53 ns fixed and 18.16 ns random on the 7600X.

input.description: Read the rest of vc-x1 push help and its commands

content.content:
Non-interactive use: pass both --title and --body plus --yes
to skip both gates.

Usage: vc-x1 push [OPTIONS] [BOOKMARK]

Arguments:
  [BOOKMARK]
          Bookmark to advance in the work repo (positional form of
          `--bookmark`). The bot repo always advances `main`.
          
          Accepting a positional lets the common case read as `vc-x1 push main`
          without the `--bookmark` ceremony; `--bookmark` is kept as an alias
          for scripts and for composition with other args. The two forms
          conflict if both supplied.

Options:
      --bookmark <BOOKMARK>
          Bookmark to advance in the work repo (flag form, see positional)

  -V, --version...
          Version detail on stdout: -V the banner, -VV the full report (as
          `vc-x1 version`). Counted like -v/-vv.
          
          Both ride along: they print, then the subcommand runs, so one
          invocation captures the version and the command's output together.
          That is why this replaces clap's auto-version, which would exit after
          printing. Without either, the banner still prints, on stderr.

      --no-banner
          Suppress the banner stderr normally carries on every run.
          
          Only the ambient banner: an explicit `-V` still prints, since asking
          for it outranks suppressing it.

      --step
          Pause between every stage for an interactive approval gate
